data.title: Insecure Kerberos Delegation Configuration
data.summary:
Systems and service accounts were configured with Kerberos delegation rights that
allowed authentication material belonging to privileged users to be captured and
reused.
data.description:
Kerberos delegation permits a service to act on behalf of a user when accessing a
further back-end service, a requirement for multi-tier applications. The security
of the mechanism depends heavily on which form of delegation is configured.

Where unconstrained delegation is enabled, any user authenticating to the affected
host has a copy of their ticket-granting ticket cached in the memory of that
system. An attacker holding administrative access to the host can extract those
tickets and reuse them to authenticate as the users concerned. The exposure is
not limited to services the host legitimately requires, as the cached ticket
grants access to any service in the domain.

An attacker can coerce a privileged system, including a domain
controller, into authenticating to the affected host, causing its ticket to be
cached and captured without waiting for a user to connect.

Where constrained delegation is configured with protocol transition, the account
may request tickets on behalf of any user without that user having authenticated
at all, extending the exposure to accounts that never interact with the service.

Hosts and accounts with delegation configured were identified within the
environment, and were not restricted by the mechanisms available to limit the
associated risk.
data.impact:
An attacker with administrative access to an affected host could capture and reuse
the authentication material of privileged users, including domain administrators,
without recovering any password. Where a domain controller can be coerced into
authenticating, this results in full domain compromise from a single compromised
server.
data.recommendation:
1. Remove unconstrained delegation from all accounts and computers. Where
   delegation is genuinely required, migrate to resource-based constrained
   delegation, which places control with the target resource rather than the
   requesting service.

2. Add all privileged accounts to the Protected Users security group and set the
   "Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated" flag, which prevents their
   tickets from being delegated under any configuration.

3. Treat any host holding delegation rights as a tier-zero asset, applying the
   same hardening, monitoring, and administrative restrictions as a domain
   controller.

4. Disable the Print Spooler service on domain controllers and other systems
   where it is not required, as it is commonly used to coerce authentication.

5. Audit delegation configuration on a recurring basis, as the settings are
   frequently applied during application deployment and rarely reviewed
   afterwards.
